name: LEEP's lead paint programmes in 13 countries (LEEP's own CEA, April 2024)
beneficiaries_note: Nothing in the model says where; the charity's main country of operation, the one its other models name most: Malawi.

missing_data.note: Thin: LEEP's projection to 2100 of rules it is helping bring in: the homes painted without lead, the children spared and their health and earnings are modelled, not measured.

summary: The Lead Exposure Elimination Project tests paint on sale in low- and middle-income countries and helps governments bring in and enforce lead paint limits and manufacturers switch. LEEP's own 2024 analysis covers its 13 country programmes: each brings enforcement forward by four to eight years, so fewer homes are painted with lead paint and fewer children grow up in them, to 2100. It counts their health (from the Global Burden of Disease, raised by half for heart disease) and their later earnings. Our view keeps LEEP's costs, children and health years, values deaths by age, and values the earnings with the site's shared figures for IQ points per µg/dL, earnings per IQ point, working years and household sharing.

sections.title: LEEP's estimate (April 2024)
sections.explainer: LEEP compares two futures for each of its 13 programme countries: lead paint rules enforced when LEEP expects with its help, or four to eight years later without it. In each, homes are painted every year (paint sales growing 5.5% a year), a share of them with lead paint until enforcement starts, after which lead paint's share falls 20% a year; the children born into the extra lead-painted homes are LEEP's impact, to 2100. Health comes from each country's Global Burden of Disease DALYs for lead per µg/dL of blood lead, earnings from IQ points lost; each country's benefits are weighted by LEEP's chance its programme succeeds. Costs and benefits are discounted at 4% a year.

sections.title: Health: deaths valued by age
sections.explainer: charityevals' step. LEEP's health years are the Global Burden of Disease's DALYs for lead: mostly years of life lost to heart disease and kidney disease in adults, at GBD's life expectancy, untouched by the value-of-life slider. Our view splits each into the illness part and the deaths behind the rest, valued by age like every death on the site.

sections.title: Earnings, valued the site's way
sections.explainer: charityevals' step. LEEP values the earnings with its own conversions: 1% of earnings per IQ point from age 15 to 64 and 2.5 years of income per DALY. The site answers each of these questions once for every model: the IQ points lost per µg/dL (facts: lead), the earnings gain per IQ point, the years it lasts and the household sharing (facts: givewell_shared), and the value of a gain in income (Your values). Our view applies them to LEEP's own count of children and the blood lead a lead-painted home adds.

sections.title: Staff pay and government money
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not LEEP's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's forgone pay and the governments' spending count in full as part of the cost.

sections.title: Bottom line
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not LEEP's: LEEP's cost per DALY-equivalent, with the health and earnings parts valued the site's way.

source.quote: we project total costs (including both charity costs and government costs) to be around $4 million.

rows.explainer: LEEP's budget for its 13 country programmes (about five to six years each) plus the governments' staff time to enforce the rules in the years they are brought forward, counted at half (LEEP: that money would otherwise be spent less well), discounted at 4% a year. LEEP states the total as about $4 million; the figure here is the one its $4.49 per DALY-equivalent and its 901,000 DALY-equivalents imply.

source.page: How cost-effective are LEEP's paint programs?
source.quote: between 2021 and 2100, LEEP's 13 programs will avert a total of 900,000 DALY-equivalents, potentially preventing 46.6 million people from being exposed to lead paint in their homes during childhood

rows.explainer: Our reading of LEEP's timing, so the discounting can follow the shared rate. LEEP's yearly profile isn't published: homes painted with lead paint in the years regulation is brought forward keep exposing the children born into them for decades. The wait is the one at which LEEP's 46.6 million children, its 83% average chance of success and its own earnings steps (1.7 µg/dL, 0.5 IQ points per µg/dL, 1% of earnings per point, 2.5 years of income per DALY, earnings from 15 to 64, 4%) give its 756,000 DALY-equivalents of earnings: 19.6 years, rounded.

source.quote: The model predicts 145,000 DALYs are averted through the health benefits

rows.explainer: Derived from LEEP's stated total, so the discounting can follow the shared rate: 145,000 discounted DALYs, less LEEP's 1.5 multiplier, undiscounted at LEEP's 4% over the 20-year wait to the exposure and the 30 years to the benefits. LEEP's own count: each country's GBD 2019 DALYs from lead per µg/dL of children's blood lead, times the 1.7 µg/dL a lead-painted home adds, for every child born into one, weighted by each country's chance of success.

source.title: LEEP, LEEP Cost-Effectiveness Analysis: Multi-Country 2024 (model documentation)
source.page: Multiplier due to cardiovascular effect underestimate
source.quote: we use a multiplier of 1.5 to account for additional cardiovascular effects in our estimate of the total DALY burden attributable to lead exposure.

rows.explainer: The GBD 2019 count of lead's heart disease is likely too low: a 2023 World Bank report puts lead's cardiovascular deaths at six times GBD's, Rethink Priorities at 30% to 100% more burden, and GBD 2021 adds 8 million DALYs. Range: LEEP's sensitivity analysis (1 to 2.5).

rows.explainer: LEEP's 145,000, at the shared discount rate (LEEP's 4% in the evaluator view): 16% of its total.

source.page: How cost-effective are LEEP's paint programs?
source.quote: The total income benefit of LEEP's activity over this time period will be approximately $43.2 billion, which is equal to 756,000 DALY-equivalents.

rows.explainer: About $43 billion of earnings the children keep: 1.7 µg/dL less blood lead, 0.5 IQ points per µg/dL, 1% of earnings per IQ point (half of Attina and Trasande's 2%) from age 15 to 64, converted at 2.5 years of income per DALY (GiveWell's). Our view values the earnings itself (section below).

rows.label: Cost per DALY-equivalent averted
rows.explainer: LEEP's bottom line: "$4.49 to avert one DALY-equivalent" (90% interval $0.78 to $12.93, from its Monte Carlo simulation), discounted costs over expected discounted benefits.

rows.label: Value of a heart-disease death averted, at the world's ages, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The ages of the world's cardiovascular deaths (facts: death_ages) valued by GiveWell's weights by age, the 70-and-over band split by the share at 80 or older, times the value-of-a-life slider, in healthy years at Your values' exchange rate. Lead's deaths are mostly heart disease in older adults.

rows.label: Our value of one of LEEP's GBD DALYs (deaths valued by age), per DALY
rows.explainer: **Changed for consistency.** LEEP counts the Global Burden of Disease's DALYs for lead (with its 1.5 multiplier for heart disease). Our view splits each DALY into the illness part (kept as DALYs) and the deaths behind the rest, at heart disease's ratio (GBD 2023, world), and values those deaths by age like every death on the site (row above). Heart disease stands in for all of lead's burden; the small intellectual-disability part is treated the same way. The evaluator view keeps LEEP's DALYs (1).

source.page: Average increase in BLL from living in a home with lead paint
source.quote: We estimate that in LMICs, child blood lead levels increase on average by 1.7 ug/dL (90% intuitive confidence interval[4]: [0.7, 3]) as a result of growing up in a home with lead paint.

rows.explainer: LEEP's estimate from studies of US homes (Lanphear et al. 1998, Clark et al. 2011, Dixon et al. 2005 and 2009), which it calls likely low. It is the dose for a child in a lead-painted home, so it stays LEEP's: the site's shared figures (a typical child's 5 µg/dL, 15% of it from paint) average over all children, painted homes or not.

rows.label: IQ points lost per µg/dL of children's blood lead
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: lead), 0.5 a µg/dL from Lanphear et al. (2005) between 2.4 and 10 µg/dL; LEEP uses the same.

rows.label: IQ points a child keeps when spared
Increase in earnings per IQ point
rows.explainer: **Changed for consistency.** LEEP assumes 1% more earnings per IQ point (half of Attina and Trasande's 2%, a little above GiveWell's); the site uses GiveWell's figure for every model, 0.67% (facts: givewell_shared).

rows.label: Household sharing multiplier on an earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared multiplier for later-life income gains shared within the household (facts: givewell_shared). LEEP counts the earner's income only.

rows.label: Years an IQ gain raises earnings, discounted
rows.explainer: **Changed for consistency.** The shared working life of 40 years (facts: givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), discounted at the shared rate; LEEP counts 50 years, from 15 to 64.

rows.label: Years from birth to working age
rows.explainer: LEEP counts children from birth into a lead-painted home; earnings start at about 20, as in our other lead models (17 years from exposure centred near age three). Our judgment; LEEP starts earnings at 15, the OECD's working age.

Governments' enforcement spending in LEEP's cost figure (half of it), discounted

source.title: LEEP, LEEP Multi-Country Sensitivity Analysis (April 2024)
source.cell: Annual government costs (base) and start of enforcement/compliance (both scenarios), rows Malawi to Senegal
source.note: Each government's yearly cost ($5,000 to $25,000) over the years enforcement is brought forward, 2021 onwards at 4%: $538,000 in all, of which LEEP counts half.

rows.explainer: LEEP counts the governments' staff time to enforce the rules at half, as that money would otherwise be spent less well: this is the half inside its cost figure (the half it leaves out is the same amount).

rows.label: Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of LEEP's cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. The governments act only because of LEEP, so they aren't co-funders: they are credited through the mobiliser's share (docs/normalization.md 2.24). Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Our healthy years for the same work, as a share of LEEP's DALY-equivalents
rows.explainer: The health years with deaths valued by age plus the earnings valued the site's way, over LEEP's 901,000. The evaluator view keeps LEEP's (1).

rows.label: Cost LEEP counts per dollar of its own (the governments' spending leaves the cost)
rows.explainer: **Changed for consistency.** The governments that enforce the lead paint limits carry out the work only because of the charity, so they are credited through the share below (mobiliser_share), not by counting their money in the cost (docs/normalization.md 2.24): counted in both, they would be cut twice. The evaluator view keeps LEEP's cost (1).

rows.label: Share of the governments' enforcement spending that LEEP counts as a cost
rows.explainer: LEEP's own rule: it counts government money at half, as that money would otherwise be spent less well (its 2021 documentation). Used here only to get back to the spending in full.

rows.label: Governments' enforcement spending, at what the money would otherwise have done, as a share of the good done
rows.explainer: **Changed for consistency.** The governments' enforcement spending in full (the half LEEP counts, over that half), valued at GiveWell's figure for what a dollar a government in its programme countries spends would otherwise have done (@givewell_shared.cf_value_government, about 1.5 times cash), the site's one figure for redirected government money (docs/normalization.md 2.20), over our healthy years gained. A cost of the resources LEEP mobilises: netted from the good before the mobiliser's share. The evaluator view counts half the spending in the cost instead (0 here).

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: DALYs averted per dollar
rows.formula: ((1 / cost_per_daly_equivalent) * ours_vs_leep * donor_cost_share) * adopter_cost_out * (1 - gov_cost_share_of_good) * mobiliser_share
rows.explainer:
LEEP's DALY-equivalents per dollar of the cost it counts, valued the site's way, per dollar of LEEP's own spending (adopter_cost_out), net of what the governments' enforcement money would otherwise have done, times the charity's share of the good that others carry out (mobiliser_share).

With credit by share of resources on, times the share of LEEP's full cost paid in cash.
